common_name: Dauntless Bearded Iris (Historic 1929 Dykes Medal Garnet-Red Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil; Dauntless is an early garnet-red tall bearded iris that became a foundational parent for later red-toned introductions.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top surface exposed to the sun in loose, well-drained soil, never burying them completely. Dauntless was hybridized by Clarence Connell of Tennessee from a cross of 'Cardinal' and 'Rose Madder' and registered in 1927, producing a garnet-red self of good size and form that was strikingly saturated for its era. It won the American Dykes Medal in 1929, the third year the award was presented, and went on to parent later Dykes winners including Ayres's 'Coralie' and Gage's 'Rosy Wings'. Divide congested clumps every three to four years after bloom, discarding the old woody center and replanting vigorous outer rhizomes.

common_name: Coralie Bearded Iris (Historic 1933 Dykes Medal Rose-Pink and Wine-Red Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil; Coralie is a historic blend iris with broad rose-pink standards flushed mauve and glowing wine-red falls.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top exposed to sunlight in well-drained soil. Coralie was hybridized by Dr. Wylie McLean Ayres and registered in 1932 from a complex cross that included 'Dauntless', the 1929 Dykes Medal winner, as a parent, producing broad rose-pink standards flushed lustrous mauve over glowing wine-red falls. It won the American Dykes Medal in 1933, one of the earliest medals to go to an iris carrying red-iris breeding from Dauntless. Divide crowded clumps every three to four years after bloom to keep rhizomes vigorous and well exposed to the sun.

common_name: Sierra Blue Bearded Iris (Historic 1935 Dykes Medal Clear Blue Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil; Sierra Blue is a historic clear soft-blue self iris known for its exceptionally smooth, refined form.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top exposed to the sun in loose, well-drained soil. Sierra Blue was hybridized by entomologist Edward Oliver Essig from a cross of 'Souvenir de Mme Gaudichau' and 'Santa Barbara' and introduced in 1930, producing an exceptionally smooth, clear soft-blue self with neat flaring falls and trim standards. After earning an Honorable Mention in 1933, it went on to win the American Dykes Medal in 1935. Divide clumps every three to four years after bloom, keeping rhizomes shallow and in full sun to avoid rot.

common_name: Copper Lustre Bearded Iris (Historic 1938 Dykes Medal Copper-and-Tan Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil; Copper Lustre blends bright copper, gold, and tan tones on a strong, hardy midseason bearded iris.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top surface exposed to sunlight in well-drained soil. Copper Lustre was hybridized by Dr. James Hampton Kirkland of Nashville, Tennessee, registered in 1931 and introduced in 1934, blending bright copper, gold, and tan tones in a strong-growing, midseason bloomer. After earning an Honorable Mention in 1935 and an Award of Merit in 1937, it won the American Dykes Medal in 1938, an early landmark in the development of brown-toned bearded irises. Divide congested clumps every few years after bloom to maintain vigor.

common_name: Rosy Wings Bearded Iris (Historic 1939 Dykes Medal Fragrant Pink-and-Copper Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil; Rosy Wings is a fragrant historic bearded iris blending deep pink and copper tones.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top exposed in well-drained soil in full sun. Rosy Wings was hybridized by L. Merton Gage from a cross of 'Dauntless' with mixed pollen and registered in 1934, producing fragrant, well-formed blooms with deep pink standards shading to copper and deep rose falls bordered in copper. After an Honorable Mention in 1934 and an Award of Merit in 1936, it won the American Dykes Medal in 1939. Divide crowded clumps every three to four years after bloom, discarding old woody rhizomes.

common_name: The Red Douglas Bearded Iris (Historic 1941 Dykes Medal Red-Toned Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil; The Red Douglas is a cold-hardy historic bearded iris from the Nebraska Sass breeding program.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top exposed to the sun in loose, well-drained soil. The Red Douglas was hybridized by Jacob Sass of Nebraska from the cross ('Redwing' x 'Cardinal') x 'Joycette', registered in 1934 and introduced in 1937, producing a midseason to late red-toned self on a sturdy 36-inch stalk bred to withstand harsh prairie winters. After an Honorable Mention in 1936 and an Award of Merit in 1939, it won the American Dykes Medal in 1941. Divide congested clumps every three to four years after bloom to keep plantings vigorous.

common_name: Prairie Sunset Bearded Iris (Historic 1943 Dykes Medal Peachy Tan Blend Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil; Prairie Sunset is a hardy historic bearded iris with a warm peachy tan blend coloring.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top exposed in well-drained soil in full sun. Prairie Sunset was hybridized by Hans Peter Sass of Nebraska and introduced in 1939, producing a warm peachy tan blend that was unusual for its era and bred for cold hardiness on the Great Plains. It won the American Dykes Medal in 1943, the second of two Dykes Medals earned by Hans Sass, the other being 'Rameses' in 1932. Divide crowded clumps every three to four years after bloom, replanting only the most vigorous outer rhizomes.

common_name: Spun Gold Bearded Iris (Historic 1944 Dykes Medal Velvety Yellow Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil; Spun Gold was the first widely noted yellow bearded iris with velvety-textured falls.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top exposed to sunlight in well-drained soil. Spun Gold was hybridized by Howard Glutzbeck, registered in 1939 and introduced in 1940, producing a tailored yellow self with an orange beard and large, deep-toned blooms whose velvety-textured falls were considered a first among yellow bearded irises. After an Honorable Mention in 1939 and an Award of Merit in 1942, it won the American Dykes Medal in 1944. Divide congested clumps every three to four years after bloom to maintain strong flowering.

common_name: Truly Yours Bearded Iris (Historic 1953 Dykes Medal Yellow-and-Cream Lace-Edged Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil; Truly Yours carries a bright yellow heart shading to lace-edged white margins.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top exposed to the sun in loose, well-drained soil. Truly Yours was hybridized by Orville Fay and introduced in 1949, producing a bright yellow heart that shades to white at the petal edges, with the entire ruffled flower finished in a delicate laced edge. After an Honorable Mention in 1949 and an Award of Merit in 1951, it won the American Dykes Medal in 1953. Divide crowded clumps every three to four years after bloom and keep rhizomes in full sun with sharp drainage.

common_name: First Violet Bearded Iris (Historic 1956 Dykes Medal Ruffled Violet Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil; First Violet carries clean manganese-violet coloring with a blue undertone on large ruffled blooms.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top exposed in well-drained soil in full sun. First Violet was hybridized by Fred DeForest and introduced in 1951, producing large, ruffled flowers evenly spaced on a sturdy stalk with clean, sparkling manganese-violet coloring touched with a blue undertone and a beard slightly lighter than the petals. After an Honorable Mention in 1953 and an Award of Merit in 1955, it won the American Dykes Medal in 1956. Divide congested clumps every three to four years after bloom to keep the planting vigorous.

common_name: Violet Harmony Bearded Iris (Historic 1957 Dykes Medal Violet Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil; Violet Harmony is a historic violet-toned tall bearded iris noted for immense, elegant flowers.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top exposed to sunlight in well-drained soil. Violet Harmony was hybridized by Edith Lowry and registered in 1948, producing immense, elegantly formed violet blooms admired for their size and refinement, later used by other hybridizers as a benchmark of iris immensity and form. It won the American Dykes Medal in 1957. Divide crowded clumps every three to four years after bloom, replanting only vigorous outer rhizomes in well-drained soil.

common_name: Blue Sapphire Bearded Iris (Historic 1958 Dykes Medal Silvery Blue Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil; Blue Sapphire is an early-blooming blue self with a light, silvery cast.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top exposed in well-drained soil in full sun. Blue Sapphire was hybridized by Schreiner's Iris Gardens from the cross 'Snow Flurry' x 'Chivalry' and registered in 1953, producing an early-blooming blue self with a light, silvery cast on a tall 40-inch stalk. After an Honorable Mention in 1954, back-to-back Judges' Choice honors in 1954 and 1955, and an Award of Merit in 1956, it won the American Dykes Medal in 1958. Divide congested clumps every three to four years after bloom to keep plants flowering well.

common_name: Amethyst Flame Bearded Iris (Historic 1963 Dykes Medal Amethyst-Orchid Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil; Amethyst Flame is an amethyst-orchid self that topped AIS popularity polls in the mid-1960s.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top exposed to sunlight in well-drained soil. Amethyst Flame was hybridized by Schreiner's Iris Gardens from the cross 'Crispette' x ('Lavanesque' x 'Pathfinder'), registered in 1958, producing an amethyst-orchid self on a 38-inch stalk that held the top spot on the AIS Popularity Poll in 1964 and 1965. After Honorable Mention and Judges' Choice honors in 1958 and 1959 and an Award of Merit in 1960, it won the American Dykes Medal in 1963, one of eleven Dykes Medals earned by Schreiner's Iris Gardens. Divide crowded clumps every three to four years after bloom.

common_name: Pacific Panorama Bearded Iris (Historic 1965 Dykes Medal Sea-Blue Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil; Pacific Panorama is a tall medium sea-blue self later used as a parent of the Dykes Medal winner 'Shipshape'.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top exposed in well-drained soil in full sun. Pacific Panorama was hybridized by Neva Sexton and registered in 1960, producing a tall, medium sea-blue self reaching about 40 inches. After a High Commendation in 1960, an Honorable Mention in 1961, and an Award of Merit in 1963, it won the American Dykes Medal in 1965, and it later became a parent of Sanford Babson's 1974 Dykes Medal winner 'Shipshape'. Divide congested clumps every three to four years after bloom to maintain vigorous flowering.

common_name: Shipshape Bearded Iris (Historic 1974 Dykes Medal Medium Blue Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil; Shipshape is a massive, easy-care medium blue self bred from 'Pacific Panorama'.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top exposed to the sun in loose, well-drained soil. Shipshape was hybridized by Sanford Babson from the cross 'Pacific Panorama' x 'Epic' and registered in 1968, producing a massive medium-blue self on a 38-inch stalk that stands out in the garden while needing little care. After a High Commendation in 1968, an Honorable Mention in 1970, an Award of Merit in 1972, and the Franklin Cook Cup in 1973, it won the American Dykes Medal in 1974. Divide crowded clumps every three to four years after bloom.

common_name: Pink Taffeta Bearded Iris (Historic 1975 Dykes Medal Rose-Pink Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil; Pink Taffeta is an early- to midseason rose-pink self bearded iris.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top exposed in well-drained soil in full sun. Pink Taffeta was hybridized by Nate Rudolph, registered in 1965 and introduced in 1968, producing a rose-pink self on a 31-inch stalk with early to midseason bloom. Before winning the American Dykes Medal in 1975, it collected a long run of honors including Honorable Mention in 1969, Judges' Choice in 1969 and 1970, and an Award of Merit in 1971. Divide congested clumps every three to four years after bloom to maintain strong flowering.

common_name: Kilt Lilt Bearded Iris (Historic 1976 Dykes Medal Gold-and-Maroon Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil; Kilt Lilt is a tall, ruffled gold-and-brown blend with maroon falls on a white ground.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top exposed to sunlight in well-drained soil. Kilt Lilt was hybridized by James 'Jim' Gibson and introduced in 1970, producing a tall, ruffled and laced bloom with standards blending gold and brown over falls of brown-maroon on a white ground, reaching about 40 inches. After a High Commendation in 1968, an Honorable Mention in 1971, and an Award of Merit in 1973, it won the American Dykes Medal in 1976, the pinnacle achievement of Gibson's career as a noted plicata breeder. Divide crowded clumps every three to four years after bloom.

common_name: Ruffled Ballet Bearded Iris (Historic 1983 Dykes Medal Blue-and-White Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil; Ruffled Ballet pairs pale blue-white standards with ruffled medium blue falls.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top exposed in well-drained soil in full sun. Ruffled Ballet was hybridized by Elvan Roderick and introduced in 1973, producing pale blue-white standards over ruffled medium-blue falls on a 30-inch stalk with mid to late season bloom. After an Honorable Mention in 1976, an Award of Merit in 1979, and the Franklin Cook Cup in 1982, it won the American Dykes Medal in 1983. Divide congested clumps every three to four years after bloom to keep the planting vigorous.

common_name: Golden Panther Bearded Iris (Dykes Medal-Winning Bronze-and-Gold Ruffled Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil; Golden Panther layers gold and bronze tones with bright golden-orange beards on heavily ruffled blooms.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top exposed to sunlight in well-drained soil. Golden Panther was hybridized by Richard 'Rick' Tasco and introduced in 2000, producing gold blooms overlaid with bronze and highlighted by darker bronze edges, with bronze-gold style arms edged in lighter lemon yellow and bright golden-orange beards on heavily ruffled flowers. After an Honorable Mention in 2002, an Award of Merit and the President's Cup in 2004, and the Wister Medal in 2006, it won the American Dykes Medal in 2009. Divide crowded clumps every three to four years after bloom.

common_name: Paul Black Bearded Iris (Dykes Medal-Winning Fragrant Purple-Blue Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil; 'Paul Black' is a fragrant, medium dark purple-blue bearded iris named for fellow hybridizer Paul Black.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top exposed in well-drained soil in full sun. The cultivar 'Paul Black' was hybridized by Thomas Johnson from the cross 'Tom Johnson' x 'Star Fleet' and registered in 2003, producing medium dark purple-blue blooms with dark orange beards and a pronounced spicy fragrance; it was named by Johnson in honor of fellow Oregon hybridizer Paul Black. It won the American Dykes Medal in 2010. Divide congested clumps every three to four years after bloom to keep plantings vigorous.

common_name: Drama Queen Bearded Iris (Dykes Medal-Winning Blackish Purple Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil; Drama Queen combines near-solid blackish cyclamen-purple standards with golden-buff-veined falls.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top exposed to sunlight in well-drained soil. Drama Queen was hybridized by Keith Keppel and registered in 2002, producing near-solid dark blackish cyclamen-purple standards over cyclamen falls showing a golden capucine-buff ground with a distinct blaze and veining, set off by rusty orange beards with a purple midline and white base. After an Honorable Mention in 2005, an Award of Merit in 2007, and the Wister Medal in 2009, it won the American Dykes Medal in 2011. Divide crowded clumps every three to four years after bloom.

common_name: That's All Folks Bearded Iris (Dykes Medal-Winning Giant Gold-and-White Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil; That's All Folks is a giant, heavily ruffled and laced gold-and-white bearded iris.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top exposed in well-drained soil in full sun. That's All Folks was hybridized by William 'Bill' Maryott and introduced by Joseph Ghio in 2005, producing giant, ruffled and laced flowers with brilliant gold standards and white falls blending to a wide muted gold band, set off by gold beards. It became known as Maryott's last iris introduction before he turned his breeding focus to daylilies, and it won the American Dykes Medal in 2013. Divide congested clumps every three to four years after bloom to maintain vigorous flowering.

common_name: Haunted Heart Bearded Iris (Dykes Medal-Winning Heliotrope Grey Ruffled Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil; Haunted Heart carries subtle pinkish-grey to heliotrope-grey tones with heavy ruffling.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top exposed to sunlight in well-drained soil. Haunted Heart was hybridized by Keith Keppel and registered in 2010, producing pale pinkish-grey to heliotrope-grey standards over falls a shade deeper with subtle shadowy veining, with inconspicuous heliotrope-to-ibis-pink beards on superbly ruffled flowers of heavy substance. It won the American Dykes Medal in 2018, Keppel's second consecutive win of the award following 'Montmartre' in 2017. Divide crowded clumps every three to four years after bloom.

common_name: Reckless Abandon Bearded Iris (Dykes Medal-Winning Tall Bearded Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil; Reckless Abandon is a tall bearded iris that shared the pandemic-combined 2020/2021 Dykes Medal.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top exposed in well-drained soil in full sun. Reckless Abandon was hybridized by Keith Keppel and registered in 2009, producing a tall bearded iris reaching about 38 inches tall. Because the American Iris Society combined its 2020 and 2021 awards cycle due to the pandemic, Reckless Abandon shared the American Dykes Medal in 2021 alongside Thomas Johnson's 'Daring Deception', one of only two years the medal has gone to two irises at once. Divide congested clumps every three to four years after bloom to keep the planting vigorous.

common_name: Don't Doubt Dalton Bearded Iris (Dykes Medal-Winning Tall Bearded Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil; Don't Doubt Dalton is a vigorous modern tall bearded iris reaching about 35 inches.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top exposed to sunlight in well-drained soil. Don't Doubt Dalton was hybridized by Tom Burseen and registered in 2014, producing a vigorous tall bearded iris standing about 35 inches tall. It won the American Dykes Medal in 2023, continuing Burseen's run of success as a modern tall bearded iris hybridizer. Divide crowded clumps every three to four years after bloom to maintain strong flowering.

common_name: Royston Rubies Bearded Iris (Dykes Medal-Winning Tall Bearded Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil; Royston Rubies is the most recently recognized Dykes Medal-winning tall bearded iris in this record set.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top exposed in well-drained soil in full sun. Royston Rubies was hybridized by Adam Cordes and registered in 2016, producing a tall bearded iris reaching about 32 inches. It won the American Dykes Medal in 2025, one of the newer winners of the American Iris Society's highest annual honor. Divide congested clumps every three to four years after bloom, discarding the oldest central rhizomes.
